metadata.title: It Was Still Learning
metadata.audience: anyone who early-stops on a flat validation curve
metadata.greeting_note: hello lexicon: Tamil, one word. Not reused — prior: Hola/Jambo, Ciao/Hej, Sawubona/Merhaba, Namaste, Bonjour, Annyeong, Olá, Shalom.
metadata.note: Track ai-. Every number comes from grokking_evidence.py, which ships here: 8 seeds, (a+b) mod 23, median over seeds, plus a weight-decay ablation. The reel claims grokking for THIS setup — a one-hidden-layer squared-activation net on modular addition — which is what the script shows. It makes NO numeric claim about large models; step counts are properties of this experiment. It does NOT claim to know which algorithm the network learned (that would need mechanistic analysis we have not done); it says only that weight decay selects a smaller-weight solution, which the ablation supports. All components verified Claude-skinned via the tokens/ check (gotcha A15). Outro is HaiTitleOutro. B03 draws NO 95% reference line: at 95 and 100 on a 0-118 axis it sat on top of the dashed training line and the two were indistinguishable, while the narration says 'the dashed line is training accuracy'. The 95% figure is in the caption.

skin_warnings: B07: palette=claude but the outro is 'HaiTitleOutro' — OUTRO LAW wants ClaudeTitleOutro

beats.narration_text: Vanakkam. This is Jainil. You are training a model. The training accuracy hits a hundred percent, the loss flattens out, and the validation number has been going nowhere for a while. Every signal you normally watch says the run is finished, so you stop it and keep the checkpoint. This week I ran a case where stopping exactly there would have thrown away a model that was about to become perfect.

show.event: composer on cream, spark + 'Vanakkam, Jainil' above it
the question types itself in
send arms terracotta, running indicator
two output lines land

props.command: Training accuracy is 100% and validation is flat. Safe to stop?
output: Flat is not the same as finished.

beats.narration_text: Here is the whole idea in one breath. A network can memorise its training set thousands of steps before it works out the pattern underneath. In between, every held-out number looks like failure. It is not failing. It is still learning, and nothing on your dashboard says so.

show.event: empty cream page, caret blinking
writer types 'Training accuracy is 100%. It has finished learning.'
writer stops on 'finished', deletes it
'barely begun' types in its place

props.text:
Training accuracy is 100%.
It has finished learning.

beats.narration_text: The task is modular addition: A plus B, modulo twenty-three. Every possible pair is one example, five hundred and twenty-nine of them. Three hundred and seventeen go into training and two hundred and twelve are held back, and no pair appears on both sides. The model is deliberately tiny — one hidden layer, ninety-six units, squared activation — small enough that nothing exotic is hiding in it.

show.event: the task card springs up as the voice names it
the model card lands beside it
both detail lists settle under their headings

beats.narration_text: Here are both curves. The dashed line is training accuracy: it reaches a hundred percent at step five hundred and never moves again. The solid line is the held-out data, and this is the part to look at. At step five hundred it sits at nought point five percent. Chance, across twenty-three classes, is four point three. So it is not merely uninformed — it is doing worse than guessing. It stays down there for another fifteen hundred steps. Then it climbs, and by step six thousand it is past ninety-five percent. Twelve times later than the moment training looked finished.

show.event: axes draw; the dashed training curve snaps to 100% almost immediately
the terracotta threshold marks step 500 — where training finished
the solid held-out curve crawls along the floor
it lifts off and climbs steeply
the held-out curve climbs past the flat training line and keeps going

props.title: TRAINING FINISHED AT STEP 500
props.caption: Training sat at 100% from step 500. Held-out reached 95% at step 6,000 — twelve times later.

beats.narration_text: So what actually moves it? Weight decay. I ran the same task four times changing only that one number. With none at all the network memorises and simply sits there: nought point nine percent on held-out data after ten thousand steps. At nought point three, ten percent. At nought point five, eighty-six. At nought point eight, ninety-nine and a half. The pressure to keep shrinking the weights is what eventually makes a smaller solution win out over the memorised one.

show.event: title, then the first bar grows — almost nothing at zero decay
the second and third bars grow as the voice names them
the last bar reaches the top and lights terracotta
caption lands

props.title: HELD-OUT ACCURACY BY WEIGHT DECAY
props.caption: Same task, same seeds, 10,000 steps. Only the decay changes.

beats.narration_text: This has a name and a paper behind it. Power and colleagues, at OpenAI, called it grokking, in twenty twenty-two. And look at the phrase they used for when it happens, because that is the whole lesson: well past the point of overfitting.

show.event: cream card, the quote reveals as the voice reaches it
citation settles beneath, smaller and softer

lines: “… improving generalization performance from random chance level to perfect generalization…”
“… this improvement in generalization can happen well past the point of overfitting.”
meta: SOURCE — Power, Burda, Edwards, Babuschkin & Misra, arXiv:2201.02177, 2022

beats.narration_text: Your turn. If there is an early-stopping rule anywhere in your training code, take this one to it: here is my early stopping configuration — help me work out whether it could have halted a run that was still improving on held-out data, and what signal other than validation accuracy I could watch instead. Patience settings tend to be inherited from whatever script you started with, not chosen.
